title: A skateboard rack, from CAD to plywood

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Skateboards leaning in every corner, a snowboard in the way, and a rental apartment where you can't drill into the walls. That was Antoine's problem in December 2021.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So he built something. What was the idea?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A vertical rack that stands on its own. It leans, so no lag bolts are needed. He needed room for six or more boards, plus a snowboard and skates, all on a cheap budget.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do you hold a skateboard upright with no hardware?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Angled slots. The design has two side panels, three horizontal ties, and six downward-angled slots per side. Decks slide in, and gravity keeps them put. He modeled it in CAD first, with dimension-driven sketches and an assembly check before buying anything.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Panels about six feet tall so a snowboard fits on the diagonal, slots about three quarters of a deck's width deep, tilted fifteen to twenty degrees. The top bay is taller with a wider slot mouth for the snowboard.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The title says plywood, but I hear there was a metal version first?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, a fun detour. In a school shop, he welded a tubular orange frame, great practice for getting things square. It proved the layout of upright posts and cross members, even if it was too heavy for a bedroom.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A Home Depot run: three-quarter inch plywood for the panels and ties, wood screws pre-drilled so the ply doesn't split, stain, and scrap two-by-fours to prop the frame while dry-fitting.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do you cut slots like that?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A spade bit makes the rounded bottom, a circular saw handles the straight cuts, and a file cleans up the edges. Then assembly, staining in a cold December garage, and a cat who inspected every flat surface.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Snowboard on top, skates in the slots, a spare on the floor. For next time, Antoine lists a steeper angle for longboards, edge banding, and a French cleat wall mount. The full write-up has the CAD render and all the build photos.
